lessons: Never generic (Daniel, Nov 17): 'garden tomato' isn't compelling. Whenever an idea just names its subject, dig deeper and research something specific and true that the niche would love: an heirloom variety and its story, an old-timer saying, a chore only growers know, a surprising fact.

Daniel (Nov 17) on 'Nana's Small Batch': no black shirts (light garments only); lettering should be folksy and soft, not bold all caps; the name/headline shouldn't be oversized and the tagline shouldn't be tiny; designs sit lower on the shirt (big ones about 7 in below the collar); mugs print smaller with breathing room.
Shop direction (Daniel, Nov 17): homemade, food and craft, feel-good homestead designs for moms and grandmas; listings written for the daughters and grandkids buying the gift.
Warm, gentle humor. Proud, never mocking. No jokes about age, weight or being 'old'. No faith or religious designs. No politics.

Look: vintage label, seed packet and recipe card styles; muted natural palette (tomato red, butter yellow, sage, cream, berry); favor serif and script/handwriting pairings; simple and readable at arm's length.
Family names (Nana, Mimi, Mamaw...) at most about 1 in 5 designs, always paired with a homestead theme, never name-only.
Every phrase must make sense on its own to a stranger. No mashups of unrelated words or headlines (Daniel skipped 'PORCH BIRD CLUB / family chapter' because it made no sense).

Daniel's placement rule: big, full-width designs start about 5 inches below the collar (never up by the neckline); SMALL designs (narrower than about 7 inches) sit lower, with the top edge about 9 inches below the collar, so they land mid-chest instead of up by the neckline. Leave layout top out and placement is automatic.
Daniel's sizing rule: tee designs print 10% smaller and hoodie designs 10% bigger than the standard fit (applied automatically per product). Big designs start about 5 inches below the collar.
Center-chest slogans and small graphics are 6 to 10 inches wide (layout width 0.5-0.8). Short phrases go toward the small end.
Full-front statement designs are 10 to 12 inches wide (layout width 0.83-1.0) and up to about 12 inches tall.
Chest designs should end above the armpit line and never reach toward the shoulder seams.
Hoodies: keep front designs compact and high on the chest so they clear the front pouch pocket.

📖 Use at most two fonts per design: one bold hero font for the main line and one plain sans-serif for the support line. Never pair two condensed fonts at similar weights, because the hierarchy collapses.
📖 Make the punchline the largest and boldest element. Keep it to a short phrase or stacked lines. A shirt is usually viewed from 3 to 6 feet away.
📖 Avoid thin strokes, because they can bleed into the fabric on dark shirts. Use script only as a small accent next to a bold primary font. Keep small text above roughly 5mm tall.

📖 Aim for a text-to-shirt contrast of at least 4.5:1 and preview on the actual shirt color. Navy on black can look fine on screen and vanish in person. Contrast with the shirt is the single biggest legibility factor.

📖 Add slightly wider letter spacing on uppercase text. Check every layout at thumbnail size before sending it to Daniel. Typography is trending as the whole design, but tiny minimal chest text is also gaining. I'll offer a bold oversized layout and a small-chest version of the strongest slogans.
📖 For every design, build separate light-shirt and dark-shirt color versions of the artwork. Don't just recolor the mockup. A design that works on white often fails on black, heather grey or navy.

📖 Keep ink and shirt far apart in value, and never use an ink close to the shirt color. That means no navy on black, no mid-gray or silver on heather grey, and no dark green on charcoal. Use black or deep navy on heather grey. Use white, cream or bright yellow on dark heathers, navy and maroon.

📖 On heather fabric, use bold, solid shapes and thick type strokes. Skip hairlines, faint gradients and soft blends, because the flecks muddy fine detail. For white type on dark heather, add a thin dark keyline.

📖 Limit each design to 2 or 3 ink colors, and 4 at most. Use light inks on dark shirts and saturated dark inks on light shirts. Keep light-ink art on dark shirts bold and simple, since a white underbase softens colors slightly.

📖 Check each design at thumbnail size on every shirt color before Daniel sees it. Only offer the colors where it reads clearly, because six good colors beat sixteen where a few look broken. In titles and tags, name the shirt color the design was made for, such as 'white print on black tee'.

Before sending any design narrower than about 7 inches, such as short slogans like 'Small plans are the best plans', check that its top edge sits about 9 inches below the collar so it lands mid-chest, and leave layout top unset so placement is automatic.

For homestead, kitchen and canning designs, default to a light garment, mixed case and a folksy font (folksy_serif or recipe_card), and size taglines at about 60% of the headline so they never read as tiny.

concept.description: A well-used pickle recipe card and a jar with a grape leaf tucked in the bottom, the old canner's trick for keeping pickles crunchy. A warm gift for the grandma, mom or neighbor whose pickles disappear first at every potluck. Printed in tomato red, butter yellow, sage and brown on a light shirt.
concept.illustration_prompt: A single centered composition in bold clean screen-print style: a slightly tilted vintage index-style recipe card with a thick deep brown #3B2A20 outline, left unfilled so the light shirt shows through as the card color, and a tomato red #B5432F header rule across the top. A few loose hand-scribbled squiggle lines in deep brown stand in for handwriting (no readable words). One corner has a soft butter-yellow #E8C766 grease-spot stain with a darker ring edge. In front of the card stands a tall quart canning jar in thick brown outline, packed with upright pickle spears drawn as sage #8A9A78 shapes. One large sage grape leaf with a simple vein pattern is tucked against the inside of the glass, with its tip peeking over the jar's shoulder. Below the card, hand-lettered in deep brown soft serif script, the words exactly: A grape leaf in every jar. Warm, handmade, flat solid shapes with thick strokes, no gradients, no background, 4 colors maximum (brown, red, sage, butter yellow).
concept.insider_fact: Old pickle recipes call for tannin-rich leaves such as grape leaves in the jar or crock, because the tannins slow the enzymes that make cucumbers go soft.

lessons: 📖 Use at most two fonts per design: one bold hero font for the main line and one plain sans-serif for the support line. Never pair two condensed fonts at similar weights, because the hierarchy collapses.
📖 Make the punchline the largest and boldest element. Keep it to a short phrase or stacked lines. A shirt is usually viewed from 3 to 6 feet away.
📖 Avoid thin strokes, because they can bleed into the fabric on dark shirts. Use script only as a small accent next to a bold primary font. Keep small text above roughly 5mm tall.

📖 Aim for a text-to-shirt contrast of at least 4.5:1 and preview on the actual shirt color. Navy on black can look fine on screen and vanish in person. Contrast with the shirt is the single biggest legibility factor.

📖 Add slightly wider letter spacing on uppercase text. Check every layout at thumbnail size before sending it to Daniel. Typography is trending as the whole design, but tiny minimal chest text is also gaining. I'll offer a bold oversized layout and a small-chest version of the strongest slogans.
study_log.topic: Typography for t-shirt slogans: font pairing, hierarchy, readability from across a room

lessons: 📖 For every design, build separate light-shirt and dark-shirt color versions of the artwork. Don't just recolor the mockup. A design that works on white often fails on black, heather grey or navy.

📖 Keep ink and shirt far apart in value, and never use an ink close to the shirt color. That means no navy on black, no mid-gray or silver on heather grey, and no dark green on charcoal. Use black or deep navy on heather grey. Use white, cream or bright yellow on dark heathers, navy and maroon.

📖 On heather fabric, use bold, solid shapes and thick type strokes. Skip hairlines, faint gradients and soft blends, because the flecks muddy fine detail. For white type on dark heather, add a thin dark keyline.

📖 Limit each design to 2 or 3 ink colors, and 4 at most. Use light inks on dark shirts and saturated dark inks on light shirts. Keep light-ink art on dark shirts bold and simple, since a white underbase softens colors slightly.

📖 Check each design at thumbnail size on every shirt color before Daniel sees it. Only offer the colors where it reads clearly, because six good colors beat sixteen where a few look broken. In titles and tags, name the shirt color the design was made for, such as 'white print on black tee'.
study_log.topic: Choosing ink colors for apparel: light vs dark garments, heather fabrics, contrast
